title: Quiz: Splines, Cross-Validation, and Missing Values

questions.text: What is the key advantage of natural splines over high-degree polynomial models for non-linear relationships?
options: Natural splines always have lower training RMSE than polynomials
Natural splines are constrained to be linear in the tails, preventing extreme extrapolation
Natural splines use fewer parameters than polynomials for the same df
Natural splines can only be fitted with glm(), not lm()
questions.explanation: Natural splines impose linearity constraints at the boundary knots. This prevents the wild oscillations and extrapolations that high-degree polynomials exhibit outside the training data range.

questions.text: In 10-fold cross-validation, the CV-RMSE curve is U-shaped. What does the left (rising) part of the U represent?
options: Overfitting — the model has too many parameters
Underfitting — too few df means the model cannot capture the pattern (high bias)
Data leakage between the training and test folds
Perfect fit on the training data
questions.explanation: The left/low-df side of the U-curve is high because too few knots means the spline cannot flex enough to follow the pattern — it underfits. Increasing df reduces this bias.

questions.text: na.exclude and na.omit both drop rows with missing values before fitting, but na.exclude inserts NA placeholders in residuals/predictions at the positions of the dropped rows.
questions.explanation: Both drop NA rows for fitting. na.exclude then 'pads' the output vectors with NA at the original positions, making it safe to cbind() residuals back onto the original data frame.

questions.text: Why are pooled standard errors from multiple imputation (MI) typically larger than complete-case standard errors?
options: MI uses fewer observations than complete-case analysis
MI adds extra parameters to the model
MI propagates uncertainty due to missingness; complete-case analysis ignores that uncertainty
MI always uses a different estimation algorithm than lm()
questions.explanation: Multiple imputation uses Rubin's rules to combine estimates across m imputed datasets. The pooled SE includes both within-imputation variance and between-imputation variance — the latter reflects the extra uncertainty from not knowing the missing values.

questions.text: The one-SE rule for choosing spline df selects the:
options: Df value that minimises CV-RMSE, regardless of model complexity
Smallest df whose CV-RMSE is within one standard error of the minimum CV-RMSE
Df that is exactly one greater than the minimum CV-RMSE df
Df value where the CV curve first becomes flat
questions.explanation: The one-SE rule is a parsimony rule: prefer the simplest model (fewest df) that is statistically indistinguishable from the best model. 'Indistinguishable' is defined as within one standard error of the minimum CV-RMSE.
